intro: Pregnancy and the first year with a baby can bring feelings nobody warned you about. This guide is for parents who want to understand what they are feeling, compare the kinds of help available, and know what starting therapy looks like. Read it in any order.

practiceNote.heading: About Ruzicka Psychology
paragraphs: Ruzicka Psychology is the Rochester practice of Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., a licensed clinical psychologist in New York. She has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. She sees adults in person at 1577 South Ave in Rochester and by video anywhere in New York.

Medical facts on each page link to their sources, such as the National Institute of Mental Health, the CDC and Postpartum Support International. For local numbers, see our study of [postpartum depression in Monroe County](/research/monroe-county-postpartum-depression).

If therapy feels like the right next step, read about [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy), [postpartum anxiety therapy](/specialties/postpartum-anxiety-therapy) or [perinatal and postpartum therapy](/specialties/perinatal-postpartum-therapy).

pages.title: Baby blues or postpartum depression?
pages.headline: Baby Blues or Postpartum Depression? How to Tell the Difference
pages.metaTitle: Baby Blues vs Postpartum Depression: How to Tell
pages.metaDescription: The baby blues usually fade within two weeks. Postpartum depression lasts longer and weighs more. Signs, timing, and when to call your provider.
pages.summary: How the short-lived baby blues differ from postpartum depression in timing, weight and day-to-day impact, and what to do if you are not sure which one you have.
pages.answer: The baby blues are mood swings, tearfulness and worry that start a few days after birth and usually fade on their own within about two weeks. Postpartum depression is heavier, lasts longer than two weeks, makes it hard to get through the day, and can start any time in the first year. If your mood is not lifting after two weeks, or it feels intense at any point, call your OB/GYN, midwife or doctor now rather than waiting for a checkup. You do not need to be sure which one it is before you call.

sections.heading: What the baby blues usually look like
paragraphs: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) describes the baby blues as starting about two to three days after birth. You might cry for no clear reason, feel anxious or upset, feel angry with the baby, your partner or your other children, or wonder whether you can handle caring for a baby. Sleeping, eating and making choices can all feel harder than usual.

The blues are very common. The MGH Center for Women's Mental Health estimates that 50 to 85% of women have them in the first few weeks after delivery, and says it may be more accurate to see the blues as a normal experience after childbirth than as an illness. Symptoms tend to peak around the fourth or fifth day and can last a few hours or a few days at a time.
Two things set the blues apart. They do not stop you from functioning, and they ease on their own. ACOG says they usually get better within a few days or one to two weeks without any treatment.

sections.heading: What postpartum depression can feel like
paragraphs: Postpartum depression is not a bigger case of the blues that you should be able to push through. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) calls perinatal depression a medical condition and says women with postpartum depression generally will not feel better without treatment. It is also not caused by anything you did or did not do.
Signs listed by NIMH, the HHS Office on Women's Health and MedlinePlus include:
items: A sad, anxious or empty mood most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks
Feeling hopeless, guilty or worthless
Losing interest or joy in things you used to enjoy
Feeling unusually angry or irritable
Trouble sleeping even when the baby is asleep, or sleeping far more than usual
Feeling little interest in your baby, or trouble bonding
Constant doubts about whether you can care for your baby
Pulling away from family and friends
Thoughts of death, or of harming yourself or your baby

sections.heading: Four questions that help tell them apart
paragraphs: You do not need every sign on that list. NIMH notes that some people have only a few symptoms and others have many. These four questions are a more useful starting point than a checklist:
items: When did it start? The blues begin in the first few days after birth. Postpartum depression can start any time in the first year, and depression can also begin during pregnancy.
How long has it lasted? The blues usually fade within two weeks. Feelings that last longer than two weeks are a reason to call your provider.
How heavy is it? The CDC describes postpartum depression as more intense and longer lasting than the blues.
Can you still function? With the blues, you can usually still get through the day. Depression can make it hard to work, run the house, or care for yourself and your baby.

sections.heading: The gray zone: two weeks in and still not sure
paragraphs: Real life is messier than a list. MGH notes that the blues sometimes lead into a more significant mood disorder, particularly for people with a history of depression. It also points out that sleep loss, appetite changes and fatigue happen to many new mothers without depression, which can make depression harder to spot.
You do not have to solve that puzzle alone. The Office on Women's Health suggests calling your doctor, nurse, midwife or pediatrician if:
items: Your baby blues have not gone away after two weeks, or they are very intense
Symptoms of depression start within a year of delivery and last more than two weeks
It is hard to work or get things done at home
You cannot care for yourself or your baby, such as eating, sleeping or bathing
You have thoughts about hurting yourself or your baby

sections.heading: What to say when you call
paragraphs: ACOG is clear that you should not wait until your postpartum checkup to bring this up. If making the call feels like too much, the Office on Women's Health suggests asking your partner or someone close to you to call for you.

You do not need the right words. Something like 'I had a baby five weeks ago and I don't feel like myself' is enough. It can help to jot down when the feelings started, how many days a week they show up, and what worries you most.

Your provider may ask you to fill out a short questionnaire such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, a 10-item screening tool. Treat it as the start of a conversation, not a verdict. They may also check for physical causes: the Office on Women's Health notes that thyroid hormone levels can drop after birth and cause symptoms of depression, and a simple blood test can check for this.

Postpartum depression is treatable. NIMH says treatment usually includes therapy, medication or both, and that with proper treatment most women feel better. [Therapy, medication or both?](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-depression-treatment-options) walks through the options, and [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy) explains how Dr. Christina Ruzicka works with new parents in Rochester and by video across New York.

sections.heading: When it is urgent
paragraphs: If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or you or someone else may be in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time.

Postpartum psychosis is rare, but it is a medical emergency. NIMH lists signs such as delusions, hallucinations, mania, paranoia and confusion. If you or someone close to you notices these, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

For support that is not a crisis line, the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is free and available 24/7: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). The Postpartum Support International HelpLine, 1-800-944-4773, is also not a crisis line. For a mental health crisis, the UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line is available 24/7 at (585) 275-8686. More local lines are on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Can the baby blues turn into postpartum depression?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. MGH notes that the blues can lead into a more significant mood disorder, especially for people who have had depression before. If your mood has not lifted by about two weeks after birth, or it is getting heavier instead of lighter, call your provider.

faqs.question: I don't feel sad, just irritable and on edge. Could that still be the blues?
faqs.answer: It could. MGH says people with the blues more often report mood swings, tearfulness, anxiety or irritability than sadness. The same timeline applies: if it lasts past two weeks or feels intense, get checked. Anger and worry can also be signs of depression or anxiety, so see [postpartum rage](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-rage) and [postpartum anxiety](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-anxiety-signs).

faqs.question: How common is postpartum depression where I live?
faqs.answer: CDC research shows about 1 in 8 women with a recent live birth report symptoms of postpartum depression. In New York State outside New York City, 12.4% of mothers reported symptoms in 2022 (CDC PRAMS data via the NYS Department of Health). Our [Monroe County estimate](/research/monroe-county-postpartum-depression) suggests about 890 mothers a year in the county are likely to report symptoms.

pages.title: Postpartum anxiety signs
pages.headline: Postpartum Anxiety: Signs It Is More Than New-Parent Worry
pages.metaTitle: Postpartum Anxiety: Signs It Is More Than New-Parent Worry
pages.metaDescription: Some worry comes with a new baby. Signs that postpartum anxiety has gone further, how common it is, what helps, and when to call someone.
pages.summary: Worry comes with a newborn. Here is how to notice when it has become postpartum anxiety, why it is easy to miss, and what helps.
pages.answer: Worry is part of caring for a newborn. It may be postpartum anxiety when the worry is constant, feels bigger than the situation, keeps you from sleeping when you get the chance, or comes with racing thoughts, a sense that something bad is about to happen, or physical symptoms like dizziness or nausea. Anxiety after birth is common and treatable. If it is getting in the way of sleep or daily life, talk with your OB/GYN, midwife, doctor or a therapist; you do not need a diagnosis to ask for help.

sections.heading: Ordinary worry versus anxiety that has taken over
paragraphs: Researchers at the University of British Columbia's Perinatal Anxiety Research Lab, in an infographic shared by Postpartum Support International (PSI), put it simply: new mothers think about their baby all the time, want their baby to be really safe, and think about danger a lot.
So the difference is less about what you worry about and more about how the worry behaves. These questions can help you notice:
items: When the baby is safe, can you set the worry down, or does it keep running?
Does reassurance help for a while, or do you need it again within minutes?
Are you losing sleep you could otherwise get?
Is the worry shaping your day, such as avoiding outings, not letting anyone else hold the baby, or researching symptoms for hours?

sections.heading: Common signs of perinatal anxiety
paragraphs: If several of those questions hit home, that is not a diagnosis. It is a good reason to talk with a professional. PSI lists these among the symptoms of anxiety during pregnancy and after birth:
items: Constant worry
A feeling that something bad is going to happen
Racing thoughts
Changes in sleep and appetite
Being unable to sit still, feeling on edge, or having trouble relaxing
Physical symptoms such as dizziness, hot flashes, diarrhea and nausea
Anger, irritability or rage

sections.heading: Panic, physical symptoms and scary thoughts
paragraphs: An ob-gyn and psychiatrist writing for the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) adds trembling, tense muscles and sweating to the picture, and notes that both anxiety and depression can cause irritability, trouble sleeping and poor concentration.
Some people also have panic attacks. PSI notes that during a panic attack you may have shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, heart palpitations, and numbness or tingling in your hands and feet.

Tell your doctor about physical symptoms, not just the worry. The MGH Center for Women's Mental Health notes that medical causes of mood symptoms, such as thyroid problems or anemia, should be ruled out before treatment begins.

For some parents, anxiety arrives as sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of something terrible happening to the baby, followed by an urge to check, clean or ask for reassurance. PSI describes this pattern as perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and says these thoughts are anxious in nature, not a break from reality. [Scary thoughts after having a baby](/guides/postpartum/intrusive-thoughts-after-baby) covers it in depth.

sections.heading: How common it is, and why it gets missed
paragraphs: A 2017 review of 102 studies, covering more than 220,000 women in 34 countries, found that about 15% of women had anxiety symptoms between 1 and 24 weeks after birth, and about 10% met criteria for an anxiety disorder.

PSI notes that perinatal anxiety can happen on its own but is often combined with depression. MGH points out that routine postpartum screening usually focuses on depression, so anxiety can be masked. If your provider asks about your mood and the questions do not quite fit, say the word 'anxiety' out loud.

PSI lists risk factors including a personal or family history of anxiety, previous perinatal depression or anxiety, thyroid imbalance, lack of partner or social support, pregnancy complications now or in the past, and pregnancy or infant loss. Anxiety can also begin during pregnancy; see [Depression and anxiety during pregnancy](/guides/postpartum/depression-anxiety-during-pregnancy).

sections.heading: What helps
paragraphs: Perinatal anxiety is treatable, and PSI suggests working with your doctor or therapist to find the right plan. The options PSI lists can be used alone or together:
items: Social support and practical help: prioritizing sleep, time for yourself, mindfulness and relaxation, asking for help, and support groups
Therapy: evidence-based approaches include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT), and others may be an option
Medication: antidepressants, and possibly anti-anxiety medicines, are the most commonly used. Talk with your prescriber or OB/GYN about the options, especially if you are breastfeeding

sections.heading: Getting support, and when it is urgent
paragraphs: One small step for this week: if someone you trust can take one feeding or one stretch of the night, let them. PSI lists prioritizing sleep as part of treatment, not a luxury.

Dr. Christina Ruzicka offers [postpartum anxiety therapy](/specialties/postpartum-anxiety-therapy) in Rochester and by video across New York, and perinatal clients may join video sessions with the baby present. She does not prescribe medication, but with your signed release of information she can coordinate with your psychiatrist or OB/GYN.

Some signs need help right away. If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby that you feel you might act on, or you or someone else may be in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. Confusion, seeing or hearing things that are not there, strange beliefs, or a sharply reduced need for sleep can be signs of postpartum psychosis, which is a medical emergency. If you or someone close to you notices these signs, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

For support that is not a crisis line, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), 24/7, or the Postpartum Support International HelpLine at 1-800-944-4773. More lines are on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Is it normal to keep checking that my baby is breathing?
faqs.answer: Checking now and then is common. The UBC Perinatal Anxiety Research Lab gives repeated checking that the baby is breathing as an example of a compulsion: something done over and over to calm a frightening thought. If checking eats up a lot of your day, or you cannot stop even when you want to, mention it to a professional.

faqs.question: Can I have postpartum anxiety without depression?
faqs.answer: Yes. PSI says perinatal anxiety can happen on its own, although it is often combined with perinatal depression. If you mostly feel wound up rather than low, it is still worth raising.

faqs.question: Can I take medication for anxiety while breastfeeding?
faqs.answer: That is a question for your prescriber or OB/GYN. PSI notes medication may be an option and that a doctor should help decide what will work for you. ACOG says antidepressants pass into breast milk at generally very low levels, and that the decision means weighing the benefits of breastfeeding against possible risks with your doctor.

pages.title: Scary thoughts after having a baby
pages.headline: Scary Thoughts After Having a Baby: Intrusive Thoughts and Perinatal OCD
pages.metaTitle: Scary Thoughts After a Baby: Intrusive Thoughts and OCD
pages.metaDescription: Unwanted thoughts of harm coming to your baby are common after birth. How intrusive thoughts and perinatal OCD differ from psychosis, and when to get help.
pages.summary: Unwanted, frightening thoughts about your baby are far more common than most parents realize. What they are, when they become perinatal OCD, and when to get urgent help.
pages.answer: Sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of your baby being hurt, even by you, are very common after birth: in one study, every new mother reported unwanted thoughts of accidental harm, and close to half had unwanted thoughts of harming the baby on purpose. Postpartum Support International (PSI) says research shows these thoughts are anxious in nature, not a break from reality, and the parent is horrified by them. When they take up a lot of time or drive constant checking and avoidance, they can be part of perinatal OCD, which is treatable. Thoughts of harm that do not feel unwanted, or any sense that you might act on them, need urgent help.

sections.heading: What intrusive thoughts are
paragraphs: An intrusive thought is one that comes into your mind when you do not want it to. It can be a picture, a phrase or an urge, and it can feel like it came out of nowhere. That is how researchers at the University of British Columbia's Perinatal Anxiety Research Lab describe them in an infographic shared by PSI.
After a baby arrives, these thoughts tend to fix on the baby. Examples from the UBC infographic include:
items: What if I drop my baby?
What if my baby suffocates in her sleep?
What if I get distracted and she drowns in the bath?
A flash of an image of stepping on the baby
A thought of hurting the baby with a kitchen knife
A sudden impulse to scream at the baby

sections.heading: Why they happen, and how common they are
paragraphs: The UBC team notes that we pay the most attention to intrusive thoughts about things we do not want to happen, and that these thoughts are more common under stress. They suggest new parents may have evolved to be extra alert to danger, which could explain why so many of the thoughts are about the baby.

In a study that followed 100 women from pregnancy to 12 weeks after birth, unwanted thoughts of accidental harm to the baby were universal, and close to half of the women reported unwanted thoughts of harming the baby on purpose. Thoughts of harming the baby on purpose were more upsetting, and they were more likely when parenting stress was high and social support was low (Fairbrother and Woody, 2008).
Dads have them too. The UBC team reports that, compared with mothers, fathers have these thoughts less often and find them less upsetting, but can find them harder to talk about.

sections.heading: What perinatal OCD looks like
paragraphs: Having intrusive thoughts does not mean you have OCD. What matters is how much room they take up and what you do to cope. PSI describes perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder as repetitive, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and urges to do certain things over and over (compulsions), often centered on the health and safety of the pregnancy or baby. Symptoms PSI lists include:
items: Persistent, repetitive thoughts or images, often about the baby, that are very upsetting
Doing things again and again to reduce the fear, such as cleaning, checking, counting or reordering
Avoiding things that trigger the thoughts
A sense of horror about the thoughts
Fear of being left alone with the baby
Being on high alert about protecting the baby

sections.heading: How to tell, and how common it is
paragraphs: When the UBC team explains how to know if it might be OCD, they point to three things: obsessions and compulsions that take up more than an hour a day, symptoms that are very upsetting, and symptoms that make it hard to manage your relationship, care for your baby, work or handle daily tasks. Only a professional can assess that with you.

Perinatal OCD may be more common than once thought. A 2013 analysis of earlier studies found that pregnant and postpartum women were more likely to have OCD than women in general. A 2021 Canadian study of 763 women, which encouraged participants to report pregnancy- and baby-specific symptoms, found that about 17% met criteria for OCD at some point in the first six months after birth, and about 7% at any one time on average. The authors say this is higher than earlier estimates.

sections.heading: Intrusive thoughts are not psychosis
paragraphs: This fear keeps many parents silent. PSI says research shows these images are anxious in nature, not a break from reality, and that parents with these symptoms tend to avoid the things they fear could harm the baby. The UBC team states there is no evidence that mothers act on their unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images or impulses, even violent ones, and the 2008 study found little evidence of a link between these thoughts and aggressive parenting.

Postpartum psychosis is different. It is rare, affecting about 1 to 2 in every 1,000 births according to PSI. It usually begins in the first two weeks, but PSI notes it can start up to a year after birth. Signs include strange beliefs, seeing or hearing things that are not there, severe agitation, a sharply reduced need for sleep, paranoia and rapid mood swings. The MGH Center for Women's Mental Health notes that in psychosis, delusional beliefs often center on the baby, and some people hear voices telling them to harm themselves or the baby. Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency.

sections.heading: When to get help right away
paragraphs: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department if:
items: You have thoughts of harming your baby that do not feel unwanted, or you feel you might act on thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
You or someone close to you notices confusion, seeing or hearing things that are not there, strange beliefs, or a sharply reduced need for sleep
You or someone else may be in immediate danger

sections.heading: Support and treatment
paragraphs: You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. If someone you love may have postpartum psychosis, PSI advises staying with them and the baby to keep everyone safe while you get help.

If you have any thoughts of suicide or of harming yourself, call or text 988 now, even if the thoughts feel unwanted. If your thoughts are about harm coming to the baby, they feel unwanted and frightening, and no one is in danger, you still deserve support soon. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA, 1-833-852-6262, 24/7) and the PSI HelpLine (1-800-944-4773) are support lines, not crisis lines. More options are on the [resources page](/resources).

Perinatal OCD is treatable. PSI lists cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure and response prevention (ERP) and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) as evidence-based therapies, along with social support and practical help. The UBC team calls CBT the most effective form of therapy for OCD, reports evidence that it works for perinatal OCD, and says it focuses on how you interpret the thoughts and what you do about them. Medication may also be an option; PSI notes antidepressants are the most commonly used. Talk with your prescriber or OB/GYN, especially if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.

When you look for a therapist, it is fair to ask how they work with intrusive thoughts and whether they offer CBT or ERP or can refer you to someone who does. [Questions to ask a perinatal therapist](/guides/postpartum/questions-to-ask-a-perinatal-therapist) has more. Dr. Christina Ruzicka's [postpartum anxiety therapy](/specialties/postpartum-anxiety-therapy) offers a warm, relational place to say these thoughts out loud.

faqs.question: Do these thoughts mean I don't love my baby?
faqs.answer: No. The UBC team found that thoughts of harming the baby on purpose tend to be the most upsetting ones, and that being upset by them is normal. Researchers note we pay most attention to thoughts about things we do not want to happen, which may be why they so often land on the baby.

faqs.question: Can intrusive thoughts start during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes. PSI describes perinatal OCD during pregnancy, after a loss and after birth. In the 2021 Canadian study, about 8% of women met criteria for OCD during the part of pregnancy it measured. See [Depression and anxiety during pregnancy](/guides/postpartum/depression-anxiety-during-pregnancy).

faqs.question: Should I tell my doctor or therapist exactly what the thoughts are?
faqs.answer: It can feel impossible, but being specific helps a professional understand what you are dealing with and what kind of support fits. If saying them out loud is too much at first, you can start with 'I'm having scary thoughts about the baby that I don't want.'

pages.title: Postpartum rage
pages.headline: Postpartum Rage: Why You Might Feel So Angry After Having a Baby
pages.metaTitle: Postpartum Rage: Why You Feel So Angry After a Baby
pages.metaDescription: Intense anger after birth can be a sign of postpartum depression or anxiety. What postpartum rage can signal, what feeds it, and what helps now and later.
pages.summary: Anger after a baby can be a sign of postpartum depression or anxiety, and it is rarely talked about. What it can be a sign of, what feeds it, and what to do in the moment and over time.
pages.answer: Postpartum Support International (PSI) lists anger, irritability and rage as symptoms of both perinatal depression and perinatal anxiety, and research has found that anger can sit alongside postpartum depression and has linked it with poor sleep and a sense of powerlessness. If your anger is frequent, feels out of proportion, has lasted more than two weeks or scares you, talk with your doctor, midwife or a therapist. If you feel you might hurt yourself or someone else, get urgent help now.

sections.heading: What it can look like
paragraphs: Anger after birth can show up early. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) notes that in the first days after birth, some people feel angry with the new baby, their partner or their other children.

It can also be present months later. A review of research on anger and postpartum depression found that mothers' anger could be aimed at themselves as well as at their children and family members, and that it could strain those relationships (Ou and Hall, 2018).
Many parents feel deep shame after an outburst. Anger is a feeling, not a verdict on what kind of parent you are, and it is a signal worth paying attention to.

sections.heading: Why anger shows up after a baby
paragraphs: Anger appears on symptom lists from several major sources on postpartum mental health:
items: PSI lists anger, irritability and rage under both perinatal depression and perinatal anxiety
The HHS Office on Women's Health lists feeling angry or moody as a sign of postpartum depression
MedlinePlus lists feeling unusually angry
The CDC notes that postpartum depression symptoms may include feeling angry
The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) lists irritability, frustration and restlessness

sections.heading: What can feed it
paragraphs: Researchers who reviewed 24 studies found three threads in mothers' anger alongside postpartum depression: anger that came with the depression itself, a sense of powerlessness, and anger when expectations were not met (Ou and Hall, 2018).

Sleep may be part of the picture. In a Canadian survey of 278 mothers of healthy babies aged 6 to 12 months, recruited for a study about mothers' and babies' sleep, 31% reported intense anger. Poorer sleep for the mother, and anger about the baby's sleep, were both linked with more anger (Ou and colleagues, 2022).

Physical causes are worth ruling out too. The MGH Center for Women's Mental Health notes that medical causes of postpartum mood problems, such as thyroid problems or anemia, should be checked before treatment begins.

sections.heading: When anger is a sign to get support
paragraphs: There is no score that tells you anger has crossed a line, and you do not need one to ask for help. It is worth talking to your doctor, midwife or a therapist if:
items: Anger comes often, or feels far bigger than what set it off
It comes with other signs of depression or anxiety, such as hopelessness, constant worry, losing interest in things, or not sleeping when you get the chance
It has lasted more than two weeks
It is hurting your relationships, or people around you seem wary of you
You feel out of control, or worry about what you might do

sections.heading: What to do in the moment
paragraphs: If anger rises while you are caring for a crying baby, the CDC's advice for any frustrated parent or caregiver applies: focus on calming yourself down, put the baby in a safe place such as the crib, and walk away to calm down, checking on the baby every 5 to 10 minutes. Call a friend, relative, neighbor, parent helpline or your baby's doctor for support. The CDC also notes that long stretches of crying are normal for babies and tend to be worse in the first few months.

If another adult is home, it can help to agree on a short phrase ahead of time, like 'I need five minutes', that means 'please take over while I step away'. Later, when things are calm, notice the pattern: time of day, how much sleep you had, whether you had eaten, and what was being asked of you. Those details are useful to bring to a provider or therapist.

sections.heading: What helps over time
paragraphs: Because anger can travel with depression and anxiety, getting checked for those is a good first step. Perinatal depression and anxiety are treatable with therapy, medication or both (NIMH, PSI). Medication decisions belong with your prescriber or OB/GYN.

PSI also lists social support and practical help, such as prioritizing sleep, time for yourself, asking for help and support groups. The Office on Women's Health suggests not trying to do everything yourself and asking your partner, family and friends for help. Ou and colleagues suggest that clinicians ask about sleep in the first year and offer evidence-based strategies to improve sleep for parent and baby, so it is reasonable to bring sleep up directly.

In [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy), Dr. Christina Ruzicka's approach is relational, psychodynamic, warm and active, and partners may be included when it is clinically appropriate and supports your goals. If much of the anger lands on your partner, [Your relationship after a baby](/guides/postpartum/relationship-after-baby) may help too.

sections.heading: If anyone is unsafe
paragraphs: If you feel you might hurt yourself, your baby or anyone else, or someone is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time.
If you are the one being hurt or threatened at home, Willow Domestic Violence Center offers free, confidential support 24/7: call or text (585) 222-SAFE (7233).
For support that is not a crisis line, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), 24/7. More options are on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Is postpartum rage a sign of postpartum depression?
faqs.answer: It can be, but not always. Anger shows up on the symptom lists for both perinatal depression and perinatal anxiety, and research shows anger can coexist with postpartum depression. A professional can help you sort out what is driving it.

faqs.question: Can rage start months after the baby is born?
faqs.answer: It can. Anger can be a symptom of postpartum depression, and ACOG notes postpartum depression can begin up to a year after birth. A 2022 Canadian survey also found intense anger in 31% of mothers whose babies were 6 to 12 months old, so anger is not limited to the early weeks.

faqs.question: Why is my anger worst with my partner?
faqs.answer: Research on postpartum anger found it could be directed at children and family members, and could be tied to expectations not being met. It can help to talk about expectations when you are both calm, or with a therapist. Ruzicka Psychology also offers [couples therapy](/specialties/couples-therapy).

pages.title: Depression and anxiety during pregnancy
pages.headline: Depression and Anxiety During Pregnancy
pages.metaTitle: Depression and Anxiety During Pregnancy: Signs and Help
pages.metaDescription: Depression and anxiety can start before the baby arrives. Signs to watch for, how common they are, medication questions, and why early help matters.
pages.summary: Depression and anxiety can begin during pregnancy, not only after birth. Signs to watch for, who is more at risk, medication questions, and why it is worth getting help now.
pages.answer: Depression and anxiety can both start during pregnancy, and they are common: in CDC survey data from states that take part in PRAMS, about 15% of women with a recent live birth reported depression during pregnancy in 2019, and a review of studies from 34 countries found anxiety symptoms in about one in five to one in four pregnant women. Signs include a low or empty mood that lasts, losing interest in things, constant worry, and feeling hopeless or on edge. Both are treatable during pregnancy, and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends counseling during pregnancy for people at higher risk of perinatal depression. Bring it up with your OB/GYN or midwife at your next visit, or sooner if it is getting in the way of daily life.

sections.heading: Yes, it can start before the baby comes
paragraphs: The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) uses the term perinatal depression to include depression during pregnancy (prenatal depression) as well as after birth. Postpartum Support International (PSI) notes that symptoms can start any time in the perinatal period, and the MGH Center for Women's Mental Health says it is not unusual for someone to have a first episode of a mental health condition while pregnant.

That can feel confusing when pregnancy is supposed to be the hopeful part. MGH notes that although pregnancy has often been seen as a time of emotional well-being, up to 20% of women have mood or anxiety disorders during pregnancy.

sections.heading: How common it is
paragraphs: Estimates vary with how and when people are asked, but the studies below all find that depression and anxiety in pregnancy are common.
items: Depression: a review of 21 studies found depression in about 7% of women in the first trimester and about 12 to 13% in the second and third (Bennett and colleagues, 2004).

Depression was being reported more often before 2020: in CDC PRAMS survey data, self-reported depression during pregnancy rose from 11.6% in 2016 to 14.8% in 2019, as cited by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.

Anxiety: a review of 102 studies from 34 countries found anxiety symptoms in about 18% of women in the first trimester, 19% in the second and 25% in the third, and about 15% met criteria for an anxiety disorder (Dennis and colleagues, 2017).
OCD: a 2021 Canadian study found that about 8% of women met criteria for obsessive-compulsive disorder during the part of late pregnancy it measured (Fairbrother and colleagues).

sections.heading: Signs to pay attention to
paragraphs: You do not have to work out whether a symptom is depression, anxiety or something else before you ask for help. NIMH advises seeing a health care provider if you have any of these signs, and a provider can work out what is causing them. Signs listed by NIMH and PSI include:
items: A sad, anxious or empty mood most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks
Feeling hopeless, guilty or worthless
Losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
Constant worry, racing thoughts, or a feeling that something bad is going to happen
Feeling on edge, unable to sit still or relax
Anger, irritability or rage
Unwanted, frightening thoughts or images, sometimes with urges to check or clean over and over
Thoughts of death or of harming yourself

sections.heading: Who is more likely to struggle
paragraphs: NIMH stresses that perinatal depression can affect anyone and is not caused by anything you did or did not do. Some things raise the risk, including:
items: A personal or family history of depression or bipolar disorder, or depression in a previous pregnancy (NIMH)
A history of anxiety or OCD, or anxiety or depression in a previous pregnancy or postpartum period (PSI)
An unplanned or unwanted pregnancy, stressful life events, or little financial or social support (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force)
A history of physical or sexual abuse, or recent intimate partner violence (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force)
Diabetes before or during pregnancy, or complications such as preterm delivery or pregnancy loss (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force)
Fertility challenges, or a previous pregnancy or infant loss (PSI)

sections.heading: Why getting help now matters
paragraphs: It is tempting to wait it out until the baby comes. An ob-gyn and psychiatrist writing for the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) notes that when your mental health improves during pregnancy, you may have a lower risk of preterm birth, a baby with low birth weight, or poor mother-baby bonding. MGH notes that depression or anxiety during pregnancy is associated with postpartum depression. That is not one more thing to feel guilty about. It is a reason to treat your mental health as part of prenatal care.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found convincing evidence that counseling, such as cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy, helps prevent perinatal depression in people at increased risk, and recommends that clinicians provide or refer them to it. It also recommends screening for depression during pregnancy and after birth. If no one has asked how you are feeling, you can bring it up yourself.

sections.heading: Medication questions in pregnancy
paragraphs: If you already take medication for depression or anxiety and find out you are pregnant, talk with your prescriber or OB/GYN before making any change. NIMH advises talking to a health care provider before starting or stopping any medication. MGH notes that many women consider stopping abruptly but that for many this may carry substantial risks; in one study of women with a history of major depression, 68% of those who stopped antidepressants during pregnancy relapsed, compared with 26% of those who continued.

An ACOG article by an ob-gyn and psychiatrist notes that medications can be taken during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and that you and your doctor should decide together. NIMH says the risk of birth defects and other problems for babies whose mothers take antidepressants during pregnancy is very low, and advises working with your provider to weigh the risks and benefits. If you have a history of depression, ACOG suggests telling your OB/GYN early in prenatal care, ideally before pregnancy.
Dr. Christina Ruzicka does not prescribe medication, but with your signed release of information she can coordinate with your psychiatrist or OB/GYN.

sections.heading: Getting support now
paragraphs: With Dr. Christina Ruzicka, support can begin while you are trying to conceive, during pregnancy, after a loss, or at any point in the transition to parenthood. [Perinatal and postpartum therapy](/specialties/perinatal-postpartum-therapy) is available in person in Rochester and by video across New York, as long as you are physically in New York for each session.

If you have thoughts of harming yourself, or you or someone else may be in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline offers free, confidential support during and after pregnancy, 24/7: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). It is not a crisis line. More options are on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Will depression in pregnancy carry on after the baby is born?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but MGH notes that depression or anxiety during pregnancy is associated with postpartum depression. That makes pregnancy a good time to start support and to plan with your OB/GYN for the weeks after birth. See [Baby blues or postpartum depression?](/guides/postpartum/baby-blues-or-postpartum-depression) for what to watch for.

faqs.question: I'm pregnant after a loss and can't stop worrying. Is that anxiety?
faqs.answer: It may be, and it is understandable. PSI lists pregnancy and infant loss among the risk factors for both perinatal depression and anxiety. If the worry is constant, keeps you up, or comes with dread or panic, talk with your provider or a therapist. [Postpartum anxiety signs](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-anxiety-signs) describes what anxiety can look like.

faqs.question: Do I have to wait for my provider to screen me?
faqs.answer: No. You can raise it at any prenatal visit, or call between visits. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends depression screening for pregnant and postpartum people, so talking about your mood is a normal part of care.

pages.title: Postpartum depression in dads and partners
pages.headline: Postpartum Depression in Dads and Partners
pages.metaTitle: Postpartum Depression in Dads and Partners: Signs, Help
pages.metaDescription: About 1 in 10 dads has postpartum depression. How it can look in fathers and partners, what raises the risk, and where to find support that fits.
pages.summary: Fathers and non-birthing partners can get depressed during pregnancy or the first year too. How it can look different, what raises the risk, and where to get help.
pages.answer: Yes. Fathers and partners who did not give birth can have depression during pregnancy or in the first year after a baby arrives. Postpartum Support International reports that about 1 in 10 dads experiences postpartum depression, and it can show up as irritability, indecision or feeling flat, not only as sadness. It is treatable, and you do not need to be sure it is depression before you ask for help.

sections.heading: How common it is
paragraphs: Postpartum Support International (PSI) reports that about 1 in 10 dads experiences postpartum depression, and that 5 to 15% develop an anxiety disorder, such as generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder, during the pregnancy or the first year after birth.

Research reviews land in the same range. A 2010 review of 43 studies found depression in about 10% of fathers between early pregnancy and the end of the first year. A 2016 update of 74 studies put the figure at about 8%. The 2010 review found the highest rates 3 to 6 months after birth, but the larger update did not find that timing made a significant difference, so the window to watch runs from pregnancy through the whole first year.

PSI also notes that perinatal mental health conditions affect not only the person who was pregnant but other family members too, including dads and partners. You do not have to be the one who gave birth for this to apply to you.

sections.heading: How it can look in dads and partners
paragraphs: Depression in fathers mostly looks like depression in anyone. But a 2019 review on postpartum depression in men notes that irritability, indecisiveness and a narrower range of emotion may show up more often in men, and that it can build slowly over the first year instead of appearing in the first weeks. The same review notes that men may be less likely to talk about how they feel, so it can go unnoticed.
Signs worth paying attention to include:
items: Snapping at your partner, the baby or people at work, or anger that feels bigger than the moment
Feeling numb, flat or far away, even in moments you expected to enjoy
Struggling to make small decisions you used to make easily
Losing interest in the baby or in things that used to matter to you
Sleep or appetite changes that go beyond what the baby explains
Headaches, stomach trouble or aches that have no clear cause
Guilt, shame or a sense of hopelessness

sections.heading: What raises the risk
paragraphs: Your partner's mental health matters here. In the 2010 review, depression in fathers was moderately linked with depression in mothers, and the 2016 update found that rates of depression in fathers varied with maternal depression. If your partner is struggling, check in on yourself too.
The 2019 review lists these potential risk factors for postpartum depression in men:
items: A past history of depression
A partner who has depression
Conflict or strain in your relationship
Poverty
An unintended pregnancy
Ongoing sleep loss, which the review says might also raise the risk

sections.heading: If you are also supporting your partner
paragraphs: Many partners spend the first year focused on the parent who gave birth, and that care matters. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) notes that spouses, partners, family members and friends may be the first to notice signs of depression in a new mother. It suggests encouraging a conversation with a health care provider, helping her get to appointments, offering emotional or practical support, and helping with daily tasks such as caring for the baby or home.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) tells new mothers to call their OB/GYN right away if they think they may have postpartum depression, or if their partner or family is worried, and not to wait for the postpartum checkup. Your worry is a good enough reason to speak up.

You also cannot carry someone else well while running on empty. Paying attention to your own mood is part of looking after your family, not a distraction from it. For how this can play out between you, see [your relationship after a baby](/guides/postpartum/relationship-after-baby).

sections.heading: Where to get support
paragraphs: Treatment research in fathers is limited. The 2019 review notes there are no randomized trials of treatment for postpartum depression in men, so clinicians use the treatments recommended for depression generally: talk therapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy, and antidepressant medication. Medication decisions belong with a prescriber, such as your primary care doctor or a psychiatrist.

PSI runs a free weekly online support group for dads, led by trained peer facilitators, for fathers from pregnancy through the toddler years, including dads figuring out how to support a partner. PSI also hosts a free weekly drop-in call with licensed mental health professionals where you can ask about symptoms and treatment without registering or giving your name. The PSI HelpLine, 1-800-944-4773, can connect you with support and resources. It is not a crisis line. For more on choosing between options, see [support groups or therapy](/guides/postpartum/support-groups-or-therapy).

Ruzicka Psychology works with women and parents across a range of identities and family structures, so you do not need to be the parent who gave birth to reach out. Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. Sessions are in person in Rochester or by video when you are physically in New York, and partners may be included in sessions when it is clinically appropriate and supports your goals. Christina does not prescribe medication, but with a signed release of information she can coordinate with your psychiatrist. Learn more about [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy).

sections.heading: If things feel urgent
paragraphs: If you are having thoughts of suicide, or thoughts of harming yourself, your partner or your baby, call or text 988 any time. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. In Rochester and Monroe County, the UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line is available 24/7 at (585) 275-8686. See [when postpartum symptoms are an emergency](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-emergency-warning-signs) and the full list on our [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Do I need a diagnosis before I ask for help?
faqs.answer: No. PSI says plainly that you do not need a diagnosis to reach out for help. A doctor or therapist can help you sort out what is going on, and the PSI HelpLine can point you to support.

faqs.question: Should I tell my partner I am struggling when they are struggling too?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes, though timing and words matter. Depression in fathers can affect the whole family, not only the father, so getting help for yourself is also a way of looking after them. If every attempt to talk turns into a fight, a therapist can help you both have that conversation.

faqs.question: Can postpartum depression in dads start months after the birth?
faqs.answer: Yes. Research on fathers covers the whole span from pregnancy to the end of the first year, and the 2019 review notes it can build gradually over that year. If you felt fine at first and are struggling now, it still counts.

pages.title: Birth trauma and postpartum PTSD
pages.headline: Birth Trauma and Postpartum PTSD
pages.metaTitle: Birth Trauma and Postpartum PTSD: Signs and Support
pages.metaDescription: A birth can be traumatic even if it looked routine on paper. Signs of postpartum PTSD, how common it is, how partners are affected, and what helps.
pages.summary: A birth can be traumatic even when it looked routine to everyone else. The signs of postpartum PTSD, who is more at risk, how partners are affected, and what helps.
pages.answer: Birth trauma is about how your birth felt to you, not only what happened medically. Feeling shaken, sad or unable to stop thinking about the birth afterward is a common reaction, and for most people it eases with time. If flashbacks, nightmares, avoiding reminders or feeling constantly on edge last longer than a month and get in the way of daily life, it may be postpartum PTSD, and it is treatable.

sections.heading: What can make a birth traumatic
paragraphs: Postpartum Support International (PSI) describes perinatal PTSD as caused by a traumatic or disappointing experience during pregnancy, delivery or the postpartum period. Examples it lists include:
items: Pregnancy complications
A prolapsed cord
An unplanned C-section
Delivery with a vacuum or forceps
Your baby going to the NICU
Feeling powerless, or without support and reassurance, during the delivery
A severe physical complication or injury related to pregnancy or birth

sections.heading: It does not have to look dramatic to count
paragraphs: A birth does not need to be a medical emergency to be traumatic. Nursing researcher Cheryl Tatano Beck studied 40 mothers' own accounts of traumatic births and concluded that birth trauma lies in the eye of the beholder. The mothers described not feeling cared for, not being communicated with, and feeling powerless, and many felt their clinicians saw the birth as routine.
So if your chart says everything went fine and you still cannot stop thinking about it, your reaction is still worth taking seriously. You do not need anyone else to agree that it was bad enough.

sections.heading: Normal aftermath or postpartum PTSD?
paragraphs: The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) says it is natural to feel afraid during and after a traumatic experience, and most people recover from those reactions over time. PTSD is diagnosed when symptoms last longer than a month and are severe enough to interfere with daily life, such as relationships or work. Symptoms usually begin within three months, but they sometimes start later.
PSI lists these possible symptoms of perinatal PTSD:
items: Flashbacks, which in this case may be of the birth itself
Nightmares
Avoiding reminders of the birth, including thoughts, feelings, people, places and details
Feeling constantly on alert: irritable, sleeping badly, hypervigilant or easily startled
Anxiety and panic attacks
A sense of unreality or detachment
Avoiding follow-up care after the birth

sections.heading: How common it is, and who is more at risk
paragraphs: A 2022 review of 154 studies covering more than 54,000 parents found that about 4.7% of mothers met full criteria for PTSD related to childbirth, and about 12.3% had significant post-traumatic stress symptoms. Rates were higher among parents who already had risk factors.

PSI lists risk factors including childhood sexual abuse or earlier sexual trauma, living through other traumatic events, a prior mental health condition, feeling powerless or unsupported during delivery, a baby in the NICU, and pregnancy or infant loss. NIMH adds that having little or no social support after a traumatic event may raise the risk of PTSD, and that getting support from friends, family or support groups may lower it.

sections.heading: Partners can be affected too
paragraphs: A partner may watch a frightening birth while feeling unable to help. NIMH notes that PTSD can follow witnessing a serious event, not only living through it, and sometimes follows learning that someone close to you went through trauma.

The same 2022 review found lower rates in fathers, about 1.2% for PTSD, and its authors called for more attention to the whole family. Sometimes two parents are carrying the same birth in different ways, and it comes out as distance or arguments. See [postpartum depression in dads and partners](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-depression-partners-dads) and [your relationship after a baby](/guides/postpartum/relationship-after-baby).

sections.heading: What helps
paragraphs: NIMH says the main treatments for PTSD are psychotherapy, medication or both, and that it is important to work with a mental health professional who has experience treating PTSD. For birth-related PTSD specifically, a 2018 review of 11 studies of women after childbirth found that trauma-focused therapies, including trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure therapy and EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing), reduced PTSD symptoms up to 6 months after birth. It found no robust evidence yet on whether they help women recover from clinically significant PTSD, and the authors say larger studies are needed. A 2024 review found that brief therapies offered soon after a traumatic birth reduced later symptoms compared with usual care, which is one reason not to wait and see.

PSI also lists interpersonal psychotherapy, social support and practical help, and medication when a doctor recommends it. Decisions about medication, including while breastfeeding, belong with your prescriber or OB/GYN.
NIMH suggests a few things you can do alongside treatment:
items: Keep simple routines for meals and sleep where you can
Tell a trusted person what tends to set off your symptoms
Set small, realistic goals
Avoid using alcohol or drugs to cope
Expect improvement to come gradually, not all at once

sections.heading: Finding the right support
paragraphs: If you avoid your postpartum appointments because the clinic or hospital brings it all back, tell your provider what makes the visit hard. PSI lists avoiding aftercare as a possible symptom of perinatal PTSD, so it is worth saying out loud.

Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. Her style is relational, psychodynamic, warm and active, with tools from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy when they fit. Use the free 15-minute phone consultation to ask how she would approach birth trauma and whether that fits what you need. With any therapist, it is fair to ask how they work with birth trauma and whether they offer a trauma-focused approach like those above. [Questions to ask a perinatal therapist](/guides/postpartum/questions-to-ask-a-perinatal-therapist) has more. She does not prescribe, but with a signed release of information she can coordinate with your OB/GYN or psychiatrist.

If you are having thoughts of suicide or of harming yourself or your baby, call or text 988 any time, and call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department if anyone is in immediate danger. See [when postpartum symptoms are an emergency](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-emergency-warning-signs) and our [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: My birth was medically fine. Can it still be traumatic?
faqs.answer: Yes. PSI includes disappointing experiences and feeling powerless or unsupported during delivery among the causes of perinatal PTSD, and research on mothers' own accounts found that trauma lies in how the birth was experienced.

faqs.question: Can symptoms start months after the birth?
faqs.answer: Yes. NIMH says PTSD symptoms usually begin within three months of a traumatic event but sometimes appear later. Reminders, such as a hospital visit, a smell or a birth scene on TV, can set them off.

faqs.question: Is it PTSD or postpartum depression?
faqs.answer: It can be both. NIMH notes that people with PTSD often also have depression, substance use or anxiety disorders. A mental health professional can help work out what is going on, and NIMH notes that treating those other conditions can also help recovery after trauma.

pages.title: Your relationship after a baby
pages.headline: Your Relationship After a Baby: Why Couples Struggle and What Helps
pages.metaTitle: Relationship Problems After a Baby: Why and What Helps
pages.metaDescription: Why many couples argue more or feel distant after a baby, what research shows, when mood symptoms play a part, and practical steps that help.
pages.summary: Why so many couples feel further apart after a baby, what the research actually shows, when depression or anxiety is part of it, and what helps.
pages.answer: Feeling further apart, or arguing more, after a baby is common. Long-term research finds relationship quality often dips after a first baby, for mothers and fathers alike, and the dip is usually small to moderate. What tends to help is naming the pattern instead of blaming each other, sharing the load out loud, checking whether depression or anxiety is part of it, and getting support early instead of waiting for things to settle.

sections.heading: What the research shows
paragraphs: In a study that followed 218 married couples through their first eight years of marriage, those who had a first baby showed a sudden drop in relationship quality after the birth, both in how they rated the relationship and in how they treated each other in recorded conversations. The drop was small to medium in size, similar for mothers and fathers, and it varied from couple to couple. It also tended to last through the following years, which is one reason to deal with it early.

A review of 37 studies found small declines in relationship satisfaction for both men and women from pregnancy to 11 months after birth, and moderate declines in the 5 studies that followed couples to 12 to 14 months. In the 4 studies that also followed newlywed couples who did not have children, those couples drifted in a similar way over the same span of time, so not all of the change is about the baby.
If things feel harder between you, you are in very common company.

sections.heading: Why it gets harder
paragraphs: For many couples, the problem is not love. It is sleep, time and patience running out all at once. A few pressures come up again and again:
items: Less sleep and less time alone together, so small irritations land harder
Roles change fast. Who does night feeds, who goes back to work, who tracks appointments: many couples never decide these out loud, and resentment builds where the load feels uneven
Identity shifts. One or both of you may miss who you were before, or feel judged as a parent
Different ways of coping. One of you may want to talk it through while the other goes quiet, and each can feel rejected by the other
Physical closeness and sex change, and partners may want different things. Your OB/GYN or midwife can answer questions about physical recovery

sections.heading: When it may be more than adjustment
paragraphs: Sometimes what looks like a relationship problem is partly a mood problem. Postpartum Support International (PSI) lists anger, irritability and rage among the symptoms of perinatal depression and anxiety, and the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) lists irritability, frustration and loss of interest among the symptoms of perinatal depression.

It can also run the other way. PSI lists marital stress and not having enough support with the baby among the risk factors for perinatal depression, and lack of partner support among the risk factors for perinatal anxiety. A review of studies on fathers found that depression in fathers was moderately linked with depression in mothers.
It is worth a closer look if:
items: Either of you has felt low, empty, hopeless or on edge most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more
Anger feels bigger than the situation, or scares you or your partner. See [postpartum rage](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-rage)
One of you cannot stop replaying the birth, or avoids anything that brings it back. See [birth trauma and postpartum PTSD](/guides/postpartum/birth-trauma)
The parent who did not give birth seems flat, irritable or checked out. See [postpartum depression in dads and partners](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-depression-partners-dads)

sections.heading: What helps day to day
paragraphs: A study that followed newlyweds for six years found that mothers' marital satisfaction was more likely to hold steady after a first baby when, early in the marriage, the husband expressed fondness toward his wife and was aware of her and the relationship, and she was aware of him and the relationship. The husband's negativity toward his wife, his disappointment in the marriage, or either partner describing their life as chaotic predicted a decline in mothers' satisfaction. Small, steady signals of care and attention seem to matter.
Some things to try:
items: Name the pattern, not the person. 'We keep having the same fight at 9 p.m. when we are both wrecked' is easier to solve than 'you never help'
Make the invisible work visible. Write down the jobs, day and night, and agree who owns what for the next two weeks. Then check in and adjust
Protect sleep where you can, for example by taking shifts. PSI includes prioritizing sleep in the practical help it suggests for perinatal depression and anxiety

Keep some time for the two of you, even short. The Office on Women's Health suggests new mothers make time to go out, see friends or spend time alone with a partner, and ask partners, family and friends for help
Try one slow conversation a week. One of you talks about one hard thing for a few minutes while the other listens and repeats back what they heard, without defending or fixing. Then switch

sections.heading: Getting help together
paragraphs: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) lists couples or family therapy, where you and your partner work with a therapist together, as one form of talk therapy for postpartum depression. You do not need a diagnosis to consider couples therapy. It is also an option when the same argument keeps coming back, resentment has built up, or you feel more like co-workers than partners.

Dr. Christina Ruzicka's couples work draws on Imago Relationship Therapy. Couples sessions are $275 for a 75-minute block, with 60 minutes face to face. Christina is in network with Aetna through Headway for individual therapy only and does not accept other insurance plans. Payment is by card, HSA, FSA or check. See [pricing](/pricing) for superbills and out-of-network benefits. Sessions are at the South Avenue office in Rochester or by video when you are both physically in New York. See [couples therapy](/specialties/couples-therapy), [marriage counseling](/specialties/marriage-counseling), [online therapy](/specialties/online-therapy) and [pricing](/pricing).
If one of you is in perinatal therapy with Christina, partners may be included in sessions when it is clinically appropriate and supports that person's goals.

sections.heading: If you feel unsafe at home
paragraphs: If your partner threatens, controls or hurts you, or you feel afraid at home, couples sessions may not be a safe place to start. Willow Domestic Violence Center offers free, confidential help 24/7: call or text (585) 222-SAFE (7233). If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 any time. More options are on our [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: What if my partner will not come to couples therapy?
faqs.answer: You can start on your own. Individual therapy is a place to look at your side of the pattern and what you need, and the free 15-minute phone consultation is a place to talk through which format makes sense right now.

faqs.question: Can we do couples sessions by video with a newborn at home?
faqs.answer: Yes, when you are both physically in New York for each session and the format fits your situation, which you can talk through in the consultation. Sessions use SimplePractice or Zoom.

faqs.question: Does arguing more after a baby mean we are not right for each other?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. Research finds that relationship quality often dips for new parents, and that couples without children drift over time too. Strain after a baby is a reason to pay attention and get support, not proof that the relationship has failed.

pages.metaTitle: Postpartum Emergency Warning Signs: What to Do Now
pages.metaDescription: In immediate danger, call 911; call or text 988 any time. The postpartum warning signs that need urgent care, and what to do right now.
pages.summary: What to do right now, and the warning signs of postpartum psychosis, suicide risk and physical complications that need urgent care.
pages.answer: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now. If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 any time, day or night. Signs of postpartum psychosis, such as hallucinations, strange beliefs or confusion, are a medical emergency even if no one has been hurt.

sections.heading: What to do right now
paragraphs: Ruzicka Psychology does not provide 24-hour crisis coverage. In any of these situations, do not wait for a therapy appointment or a call back.
items: Immediate danger, or you cannot keep yourself or someone else safe: call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.
Thoughts of suicide, or of harming yourself or your baby: call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It is free, confidential and open 24/7. If you might act on the thoughts, call 911.
Signs of psychosis in a new parent: call 911 or go to the emergency department, and stay with the parent and the baby so everyone is safe.
Someone has attempted suicide: call 911 right away and do not leave them alone, even after you have called.
In Rochester and Monroe County, you can also call the UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line at (585) 275-8686, 24/7.
Tell responders and doctors if you gave birth or were pregnant in the past year.

sections.heading: Signs of postpartum psychosis
paragraphs: Postpartum psychosis is rare, about 1 to 2 in every 1,000 births, according to Postpartum Support International (PSI). The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) calls it a psychiatric emergency that requires hospitalization. PSI says it usually starts in the first two weeks after birth but can happen up to a year later. Signs include:
items: Seeing, hearing or smelling things that are not there
Delusions: strange beliefs or beliefs that are not true
Confusion, or trouble communicating at times
Paranoia and suspiciousness
A high, elated or very agitated mood, hyperactivity or more energy than usual, or rapid mood swings
A decreased need for sleep, or being unable to sleep
Severe depression or lack of emotion

sections.heading: Who is more at risk, and why family should act
paragraphs: PSI says the biggest risk factor is a personal or family history of bipolar disorder or a previous psychotic episode, and that going days without sleep may also raise the risk. Most people with postpartum psychosis do not harm themselves or anyone else, PSI notes, but psychosis affects judgment, so there is always a risk of danger. A partner or relative may need to be the one who makes the call. NIMH says recovery is possible with professional help.

sections.heading: Warning signs of suicide
paragraphs: NIMH lists these among the signs that someone may be thinking about suicide. Get help as soon as possible, especially if a sign is new or getting worse:
items: Talking about wanting to die, great guilt or shame, or being a burden to others
Feeling empty, hopeless, trapped or that there is no reason to live
Feeling unbearable emotional or physical pain
Making a plan or researching ways to die
Withdrawing from friends, saying goodbye or giving important things away
Using drugs or alcohol more often, or taking dangerous risks
Extreme mood swings, or feeling extremely sad, more anxious, agitated or full of rage

sections.heading: Frightening thoughts: when they need urgent help
paragraphs: Some new parents have sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of harm coming to the baby. PSI describes these intrusive thoughts in perinatal OCD as anxious in nature, not a break from reality, and says parents feel a sense of horror about them and may avoid situations they fear. They deserve care: tell your provider about them right away.

Treat it as an emergency, and call 911 or go to the emergency department, if you are afraid you may act on the thoughts, or if they come with confusion, hearing or seeing things others do not, or beliefs that are not true. More in [scary thoughts after having a baby](/guides/postpartum/intrusive-thoughts-after-baby).

sections.heading: Physical warning signs count too
paragraphs: The CDC lists urgent maternal warning signs that need medical care immediately, during pregnancy and up to a year after birth. Besides thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, they include:
items: A headache that will not go away or gets worse over time
Dizziness or fainting
Changes in your vision
A fever of 100.4°F or higher
Extreme swelling of your hands or face
Trouble breathing, chest pain or a fast-beating heart
Severe nausea and throwing up
Severe belly pain that does not go away
Heavy bleeding after birth (soaking through one or more pads in an hour, or passing clots bigger than an egg or tissue), or vaginal discharge that smells bad
Severe swelling, redness or pain in a leg or arm
Overwhelming tiredness
During pregnancy: your baby's movements stop or slow down, or you have vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking

sections.heading: Support lines that are not crisis lines
paragraphs: When you are not in immediate danger: the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), call or text, 24/7, and the Postpartum Support International HelpLine, 1-800-944-4773. Neither is a crisis line. If you feel unsafe at home, Willow Domestic Violence Center is available by call or text at (585) 222-SAFE (7233). The full list is on our [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Can therapy take the place of the emergency room?
faqs.answer: No. Therapy is not emergency care, and Ruzicka Psychology refers out crisis care. Once the emergency has been handled, PSI says people who have had postpartum psychosis should continue with a doctor and therapist, and ongoing therapy can be part of that care.

faqs.question: What if I am not sure it is serious?
faqs.answer: Call anyway. The CDC advises talking to your health care provider if something just does not feel right or you are not sure, and telling them you were pregnant in the past year. You can also call or text 988 at any hour for emotional distress, not only for a suicidal crisis.

faqs.question: What if my depression gets worse after starting medication?
faqs.answer: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says that if depression gets worse soon after starting medication, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself or others, call your OB/GYN, another health care professional or emergency services right away.
