pages.title: Therapy, medication or both?
pages.headline: Therapy, Medication or Both? Treatment Options for Postpartum Depression
pages.metaTitle: Postpartum Depression Treatment: Therapy, Medication or Both
pages.metaDescription: How talk therapy, antidepressants and zuranolone compare for postpartum depression, plus questions to bring to your OB/GYN or prescriber.
pages.summary: How talk therapy and medication compare for postpartum depression, what changes if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and how to decide with your providers.
pages.answer: Postpartum depression is treatable, and treatment usually means talk therapy, medication, or both together. Several kinds of therapy have good evidence, antidepressants can help alone or alongside therapy, and there is an FDA-approved pill made specifically for postpartum depression. The right mix depends on how severe things feel, your history, whether you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and what you prefer, so make the medication part of the decision with your OB/GYN, primary care doctor or psychiatrist.

sections.heading: The short version: three main routes
paragraphs: The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) says treatment for perinatal depression usually includes therapy, medication, or a combination of the two, and that with proper treatment most women feel better. It also says women with postpartum depression generally will not feel better without treatment, which is why waiting it out is not one of the routes.

Support matters too. The HHS Office on Women's Health lists therapy, support groups, self-care, help from people you trust and medication as ways to get help that can be used alone or together. Groups are covered in [Support groups or therapy?](/guides/postpartum/support-groups-or-therapy).

sections.heading: What talk therapy offers
paragraphs: In talk therapy you meet with a mental health professional, talk about what you are feeling and work out how to manage it. ACOG notes it can be one-on-one, in a group led by a therapist, or with a partner or family, and that it may last a few weeks or a few months or longer.

NIMH names two evidence-based approaches for perinatal depression: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which works on unhelpful thoughts and behaviors, and interpersonal therapy (IPT), which works on relationships, support and life changes. Postpartum Support International (PSI) adds that other approaches may also be an option, so it is fair to ask any therapist how they work.

Therapy can also start before symptoms take hold. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends counseling, mainly CBT and IPT, for pregnant and postpartum people at increased risk, such as those with a history of depression, and found convincing evidence that it helps prevent perinatal depression.
What therapy cannot do is prescribe. Many therapists, including Dr. Christina Ruzicka, do not prescribe medication, so if you want both, you will have two people on your team.

sections.heading: What medication offers
paragraphs: Antidepressants can effectively treat perinatal depression on their own or combined with therapy, according to NIMH. They take time: NIMH says usually 4–8 weeks, and sleep, appetite and concentration often improve before mood lifts. You may need to try more than one.

Side effects are possible. ACOG says most are temporary and to call your OB/GYN or another health professional if side effects are severe or unusual. If depression worsens soon after starting, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself or others, ACOG says to call your OB/GYN, another health professional or emergency medical services right away. You can also call or text 988 at any time. NIMH adds that, in some cases, people under 25 may have an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior on antidepressants, especially in the first few weeks or after a dose change, and that the FDA advises watching people of all ages closely during the first few weeks.

In August 2023 the FDA approved zuranolone (brand name Zurzuvae), the first pill approved to treat postpartum depression in adults. In November 2026 the FDA updated its label to include people 15 and older. It is taken once a day at bedtime with food that contains fat, for 14 days. In two placebo-controlled studies, people taking it improved significantly more than those on placebo at day 15, and the difference held at day 42.

Zuranolone carries a boxed warning: do not drive or operate heavy machinery for at least 12 hours after a dose. The FDA lists drowsiness, dizziness, diarrhea, fatigue, cold symptoms and urinary tract infections as the most common side effects, and it may cause suicidal thoughts. Because it may harm a fetus, the FDA says to use effective contraception while taking it and for one week after.

You may also read about brexanolone, an IV medicine for postpartum depression given during a brief hospital stay. The FDA withdrew its approval in April 2025 after the maker said it was no longer marketed.

sections.heading: If you are pregnant or breastfeeding
paragraphs: This is where many parents feel stuck, and it deserves a direct conversation with your prescriber. NIMH says the risk of birth defects and other problems for babies whose mothers take antidepressants during pregnancy is very low, and that you should tell your provider if you are pregnant or nursing so you can weigh the risks and benefits together.

Antidepressants pass into breast milk, and ACOG says the levels are generally very low; deciding means weighing the benefits of breastfeeding against the baby's exposure. The Office on Women's Health notes that some antidepressants can be taken while breastfeeding. Zuranolone also passes into breast milk, and ACOG says it is not clear how it affects milk supply or babies; you may be able to keep breastfeeding during the 14 days, or pause until a week after the last dose.

If you have had depression before, tell your OB/GYN early, ideally before pregnancy. ACOG says they may suggest starting treatment right after birth to prevent postpartum depression. NIMH's advice holds throughout: talk to a provider before starting or stopping any medication.

sections.heading: How to decide what fits you
paragraphs: There is no single right answer, and PSI says the medication decision belongs to you and your medical professional together. These questions can make that conversation easier.
items: How much is this affecting daily life: sleep, eating, caring for yourself or the baby, work?
Have you had depression or anxiety before, and what helped? PSI notes that if a medication worked well for you before, it may be worth considering again.
Are you pregnant, breastfeeding or planning another pregnancy?
Would you rather start with therapy, with medication, or with both at once?
Could something physical be adding to it? The Office on Women's Health notes thyroid levels can drop after birth, and a simple blood test can check.
How will you and your providers know the plan is working, and when will you check in?

sections.heading: When weekly therapy is not enough
paragraphs: Some people need more than a weekly appointment. PSI describes intensive outpatient and partial hospitalization programs as part-time programs where you live at home and attend treatment during the day, and inpatient care as short-term, round-the-clock treatment in a hospital.

Postpartum psychosis is different from depression. NIMH calls it a psychiatric emergency that requires hospitalization. Signs include confusion, seeing or hearing things that are not there, and beliefs that are not true.

If you or anyone else is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time. In Monroe County, the UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line is (585) 275-8686, 24/7. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), takes calls and texts 24/7 but is not a crisis line. More numbers are on the [resources page](/resources).

sections.heading: Where Ruzicka Psychology fits
paragraphs: Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., is a Licensed Clinical Psychologist in Rochester who has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. She provides therapy, not medication: she does not prescribe, and with your signed release of information she coordinates with your psychiatrist or OB/GYN.

Her style is relational, psychodynamic, warm and active, with tools from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy when they fit. She refers out crisis care and conditions that need a high level of care, and the practice does not provide 24-hour crisis coverage. Read more about [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy).

faqs.question: Can I treat postpartum depression with therapy alone?
faqs.answer: Therapy alone is one of the usual routes. NIMH lists therapy, medication or both as the usual options and names CBT and IPT as evidence-based. If your symptoms are severe, getting worse, or not easing, talk with your doctor about adding medication.

faqs.question: Do I have to stop breastfeeding to take medication?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. PSI says people can breastfeed and take medication, and that the decision should be made with a provider who knows the current research. ACOG says antidepressant levels in breast milk are generally very low. Ask your prescriber about the specific medicine.

faqs.question: Can my therapist tell me whether I need medication?
faqs.answer: A therapist can help you notice how symptoms are changing and encourage a medical evaluation, but the medication decision belongs with a prescriber such as your OB/GYN, primary care doctor or a psychiatrist. Christina does not prescribe; she can coordinate with your prescriber once you sign a release.

pages.title: Do you need a perinatal therapist?
pages.headline: Do You Need a Perinatal Therapist? What Perinatal Training Means
pages.metaTitle: Do You Need a Perinatal Therapist? What Training Means
pages.metaDescription: What 'perinatal therapist' means, how PSI training and the PMH-C credential work, how to check a New York license, and when perinatal training matters most.
pages.summary: What the perinatal label does and does not tell you, how to check a therapist's license and training, and when perinatal experience matters most.
pages.answer: You don't strictly need one, but it can help. 'Perinatal therapist' is not a license: it usually means a licensed therapist who has taken extra training in mental health during pregnancy and the first year after birth, such as Postpartum Support International's courses or its PMH-C certification. PSI says talking with a therapist who understands perinatal mental health conditions can be extremely beneficial. Check the license first, then ask what perinatal training they have and how they use it.

sections.heading: What 'perinatal' actually means
paragraphs: Perinatal means the time all around birth. Postpartum Support International (PSI) uses it for all of pregnancy and the baby's first year. A perinatal therapist focuses on that window: depression and anxiety in pregnancy or after birth, frightening intrusive thoughts, birth trauma, loss, and the strain a new baby can put on a relationship.

There is no separate license for this. In New York, therapy is provided by licensed professionals such as psychologists, licensed clinical social workers (LCSW), mental health counselors (LMHC) and marriage and family therapists, all licensed through the State Education Department's Office of the Professions. Perinatal training is an addition to that license, not a replacement for it.

sections.heading: Start with the license
paragraphs: A license is the baseline. You can look up any New York license, and any public enforcement actions, with the Office of the Professions [online verification search](https://eservices.nysed.gov/professions/verification-search). It takes a minute.

Prescribing is separate. Many therapists do not prescribe medication. If you may want medication, you will also need a prescriber, such as an OB/GYN, primary care doctor, psychiatrist or psychiatric nurse practitioner, and it helps when your therapist and prescriber can talk with each other, with your written permission. [Therapy, medication or both?](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-depression-treatment-options) compares the options.

sections.heading: What perinatal training looks like
paragraphs: PSI offers perinatal mental health training for professionals and runs the Perinatal Mental Health Certification, known as PMH-C. According to PSI, applicants on the therapy track need a graduate degree, two years of work experience that includes perinatal clients, and 20 hours of perinatal mental health training: a foundational course of at least 14 hours plus at least 6 hours of advanced training.

After their documents are verified and their application is approved, applicants register for the exam. People who pass can put PMH-C after their name, and they must complete 12 continuing education hours every two years to keep it. In May 2026 the program was accredited by the National Commission for Certifying Agencies.

PMH-C is a credential from a professional organization, not a state license. Training of any kind is one signal, not proof of skill, so ask what a therapist's training covered and how it shapes their work.

sections.heading: When perinatal training matters most
paragraphs: A good general therapist can help with a lot. Perinatal training tends to matter more when:
items: You are having unwanted, frightening thoughts about your baby. PSI describes these thoughts in perinatal OCD as anxious in nature, not a break from reality. A therapist should know how this differs from postpartum psychosis, which NIMH calls a psychiatric emergency. Get help right away if you are afraid you might act on a thought, or if you or others notice confusion or seeing or hearing things that are not there: call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department, and call or text 988 at any time. See [scary thoughts after having a baby](/guides/postpartum/intrusive-thoughts-after-baby).
Symptoms started in pregnancy, or after a loss, a difficult birth or a NICU stay.
You have questions about medication while pregnant or breastfeeding and want a therapist who can work alongside your prescriber.
You are a dad or partner and not sure your experience counts. PSI notes that perinatal mental health conditions also affect dads and partners.
Your relationship, sleep, feeding and sense of who you are all feel tangled together.

sections.heading: How to find and check a perinatal therapist
paragraphs: A few places to start:
items: Ask your OB/GYN, midwife or your baby's pediatrician who they refer to.
Search PSI's online provider directory. PSI says listed providers are in good standing with state or province standards and have completed perinatal mental health training.
Call or text the PSI HelpLine at 1-800-944-4773 for information and resources. It is not a crisis line.
Check the license on the New York State Office of the Professions verification search.
If a practice offers a free consultation call, use it to ask your questions.

sections.heading: Questions are part of choosing
paragraphs: PSI's FAQ says you have the right and the responsibility to ask about a therapist's qualifications, training, approach to treatment and confidentiality policies. It is not rude, and a good fit is worth a few minutes of questions. Our list of [questions to ask a perinatal therapist](/guides/postpartum/questions-to-ask-a-perinatal-therapist) covers training, approach, babies in sessions, fees and what happens in a crisis.

Therapy is not emergency care. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time. More numbers are on the [resources page](/resources).

sections.heading: Where Ruzicka Psychology fits
paragraphs: Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., is a Licensed Clinical Psychologist, New York license 024357. She has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. She does not hold the PMH-C credential.

She works with adults 18 and older, women and parents across a range of identities and family structures. Support can begin while trying to conceive, during pregnancy, after a loss, following birth, or at any point in the transition to parenthood. Her style is relational, psychodynamic, warm and active, with tools from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy when they fit.

Sessions are in person at 1577 South Ave in Rochester or virtual anywhere in New York. She does not prescribe, and she refers out crisis care and conditions that need a high level of care. More on [perinatal and postpartum therapy](/specialties/perinatal-postpartum-therapy).

faqs.question: Is PMH-C the same as a license?
faqs.answer: No. A New York license is what allows someone to practice as a psychologist, social worker or counselor here. PMH-C is a certification from Postpartum Support International that reflects perinatal training, experience and a passed exam. Check the license first, then ask about perinatal training.

faqs.question: Does a therapist need PMH-C to help with postpartum depression?
faqs.answer: No. PMH-C is one way to show perinatal training, not a requirement to treat postpartum depression. Ask what training a therapist has done, PMH-C or otherwise, and how it shows up in their work.

faqs.question: Can a perinatal therapist see my partner too?
faqs.answer: Practices differ, so ask. At Ruzicka Psychology, partners and babies may be included in sessions when it is clinically appropriate and supports your goals, and Christina's couples work draws on Imago Relationship Therapy. See [your relationship after a baby](/guides/postpartum/relationship-after-baby).

pages.title: Support groups or therapy?
pages.headline: Support Groups or Therapy After a Baby? How to Choose
pages.metaTitle: Support Groups or Therapy After a Baby? How to Choose
pages.metaDescription: How Postpartum Support International's free online groups compare with therapy after a baby, when a group is a good first step, and when to get more help.
pages.summary: What PSI's free online support groups offer, what therapy adds, what the research says about each, and how to tell whether a group alone is enough for now.
pages.answer: They do different jobs, and many parents use both. A peer support group connects you with other parents who understand; Postpartum Support International (PSI) runs free online groups led by trained peer facilitators, and you don't need a diagnosis to join. Therapy is treatment with a licensed professional. If you mainly feel isolated or are adjusting, and you are still getting through your days, a group can be a good place to start; mention how you are feeling to your doctor, nurse or midwife too. If symptoms last more than two weeks, keep getting worse or make it hard to function, a group should not be your only support.

sections.heading: What PSI's online support groups are like
paragraphs: PSI runs more than 50 free online support groups. They meet on Zoom through a platform called ShareWell, they are confidential, and students and clinicians are not allowed to sit in and observe.

Most groups last 90 minutes. According to PSI, the first half hour covers information, education and group guidelines, and the next hour is talk time. You need to be there for the guidelines before joining the conversation, and up to 16 people are admitted, so arriving on time matters. PSI's FAQ says you can share or simply listen.

The perinatal mood group for moms and birthing people is led by trained peer facilitators with lived experience, and you don't need a diagnosis to attend. There are also groups for specific situations, including:
items: Pregnancy mood support, and perinatal mood support up to two years after birth
Dads, and parents of babies who are or were in the NICU
Birth trauma, perinatal OCD and postpartum rage
Queer and trans parents, and single parents
Pregnancy and infant loss

sections.heading: What therapy does that a group does not
paragraphs: A peer group is support, not treatment. PSI says plainly that support groups are not a substitute for professional care, and MedlinePlus says support groups may be helpful but should not replace medicine or talk therapy if you have postpartum depression.

Therapy is private time with a licensed professional who can assess what is going on, build a plan around your history, use approaches with evidence behind them, and coordinate with your doctor if medication is part of the picture. NIMH names cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy as evidence-based for perinatal depression.

There is also a middle option. ACOG lists group therapy, where you meet with a therapist and other people with similar concerns, as one form of talk therapy. That is different from a peer-led support group.

sections.heading: What the research says
paragraphs: Studies of peer support are encouraging but mixed. A 2025 review of 19 randomized trials with 3,821 participants found that peer-led help overall improved perinatal depression symptoms compared with usual care. The largest effects came from structured therapy delivered by trained peers. For peer discussion groups, the effect was small and not clearly different from usual care, although the authors' subgroup analyses suggested group interventions may lead to the greatest improvement. Peer help overall did not clearly improve anxiety, but peer-delivered therapy did.

An earlier review of 10 trials also found peer support reduced depression scores, and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force has called for more and larger trials of peer counseling. The honest summary: groups offer connection and a chance to meet people who have recovered, as PSI puts it, while the evidence that a discussion group alone treats depression is thin.

sections.heading: When a group may be a good first step
paragraphs: A group is a reasonable first step, alongside a check-in with your doctor, nurse or midwife, when:
items: What you mostly feel is lonely, or you want to hear from parents who have been through it.

You are in the first couple of weeks after birth with mood swings and tearfulness that come and go. PSI cites an estimate that about 80% of new parents have these in the first two to three weeks, and they pass without medical treatment.
You are still sleeping when you can, eating, and managing the basics of caring for yourself and your baby.
You have no thoughts of harming yourself or your baby.
You want something free and flexible while you see how things go.

sections.heading: Signs a group should not be your only support
paragraphs: The HHS Office on Women's Health says to call your doctor, nurse, midwife or pediatrician if:
items: Baby blues symptoms do not go away after two weeks, or are very intense
Symptoms of depression begin within a year of delivery and last more than two weeks
It is hard to work or get things done at home
You cannot care for yourself or your baby, such as eating, sleeping or bathing
You have thoughts about hurting yourself or your baby

sections.heading: Getting help now, and using both
paragraphs: Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or signs such as confusion or seeing or hearing things that are not there, need urgent help. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time. PSI groups and the PSI HelpLine (1-800-944-4773) are not crisis services. More numbers are on the [resources page](/resources).

Outside a crisis, you don't have to choose. The Office on Women's Health says therapy, support groups and other help can be used alone or together. A group can give you connection between sessions while therapy does the deeper work, and a group can keep you company while you look for a therapist or after therapy ends.

PSI also offers a peer mentor program that matches you with a trained volunteer who has recovered from a similar experience, and a weekly drop-in call led by licensed mental health professionals where you can ask about symptoms and treatment without registering or giving your name. The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), offers free, confidential support by call or text, 24/7; it is not a crisis line.

sections.heading: If you want therapy in Rochester
paragraphs: You are far from the only parent here. Our [Monroe County estimate](/research/monroe-county-postpartum-depression) suggests about 890 mothers in the county are likely to report postpartum depression symptoms each year.

Dr. Christina Ruzicka offers individual therapy at her office on South Avenue in Rochester and virtually across New York, and perinatal clients may join virtual sessions with the baby present. She has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam. If you are not sure whether you need therapy or a group, the free 15-minute phone consultation is a place to talk it through. See [postpartum depression therapy](/specialties/postpartum-depression-therapy) or [postpartum anxiety therapy](/specialties/postpartum-anxiety-therapy).

faqs.question: Do I have to talk in a PSI group?
faqs.answer: No. PSI says you can share or simply listen. You do need to be there for the group guidelines at the start before joining the conversation.

faqs.question: Are PSI support groups therapy?
faqs.answer: No. They are peer support led by trained facilitators, and PSI says they are not a substitute for professional care. They can sit alongside therapy.

faqs.question: Is there a group for dads or partners?
faqs.answer: Yes. PSI runs a Dad Support Group for dads of newborns up to toddlers, a perinatal mood group for parents, and a Queer and Trans Parent Support Group. Read more in [postpartum depression in dads and partners](/guides/postpartum/postpartum-depression-partners-dads).

pages.summary: The three ways people pay for therapy, what to ask your insurer before you start, and exactly what Ruzicka Psychology charges and accepts.
pages.answer: Most people pay for therapy in one of three ways: through an in-network insurance plan, by paying the practice and claiming out-of-network reimbursement with a superbill, or by paying out of pocket, sometimes at a reduced sliding-scale fee. At Ruzicka Psychology in Rochester, individual therapy is $225 per session, Christina is in network with Aetna through Headway for individual therapy only, and a superbill is sent each month if you want to claim out-of-network benefits. Whether your insurer pays anything back depends on your plan, so check before you start.

sections.heading: Three ways to pay
paragraphs: When you are exhausted, money questions can feel like one more thing. It helps to know which of these three routes you are on before the first session.
items: In network: the therapist has a contract with your insurance plan. You usually pay a copay or coinsurance, and you may have a deductible to meet first. A deductible is the amount you pay for covered care before your plan starts to pay.

Out of network: you pay the therapist, then send a superbill to your insurer. If your plan has out-of-network benefits, it may pay back a percentage of what it considers the allowed amount, possibly after you meet a deductible; some plans have separate deductibles for certain services.
Self-pay: you pay the fee directly and don't involve insurance. Some practices offer reduced sliding-scale fees for self-pay clients.

sections.heading: If you have Aetna
paragraphs: Christina is in network with Aetna through Headway for individual therapy only. She does not take any other insurance plans, and couples therapy is not part of the Aetna arrangement.

Before you start, call the member services number on your Aetna card and ask what you will pay for outpatient therapy with an in-network psychologist: your copay or coinsurance, whether you have a deductible to meet, and whether you need a referral or prior authorization.

sections.heading: Out-of-network benefits and superbills
paragraphs: A superbill is an itemized receipt for your sessions that you send to your insurer to ask for reimbursement. Ruzicka Psychology sends one automatically each month, or weekly if you ask.

Whether you get anything back, and how much, is up to your plan. Some plans, such as many HMO and EPO plans, generally don't cover out-of-network care except in an emergency. Others pay a percentage of the plan's allowed amount, which can be lower than the $225 fee, and only after any out-of-network deductible is met. HealthCare.gov notes that out-of-network coinsurance usually costs you more than in-network coinsurance. Only your insurer can tell you what it will pay.
Questions to ask your insurer:
items: Do I have out-of-network benefits for outpatient therapy with a licensed psychologist?
Is there an out-of-network deductible, and how much of it have I met this year?
What percentage of the allowed amount do you reimburse?
Do I need a referral or prior authorization?
How do I submit a superbill, and is there a claim form?

sections.heading: Ruzicka Psychology's fees
paragraphs: Here is what the practice charges and accepts. The [pricing page](/pricing) walks through the insurance questions step by step.
items: Individual therapy: $225 per 60-minute block, with 45–50 minutes face to face and 10–15 minutes for documentation and treatment planning. The first session is the same rate.
Couples therapy: $275 per 75-minute block, with 60 minutes face to face.
The 15-minute phone consultation before you start is free.
Payment by card, HSA, FSA or check.
Cancellations need 24 hours' notice, or the full fee applies.

sections.heading: Planning your budget
paragraphs: Most clients begin weekly and may move to every other week later, so plan for weekly sessions at first. At the full $225 fee, four weekly individual sessions come to $900. How long therapy lasts varies, from short-term focused work to longer-term therapy, and you and Christina review it together.

On HSAs and FSAs: IRS Publication 502 lists amounts you pay a psychologist for medical care as a medical expense, and IRS Publication 969 explains that HSA and health FSA money can be used for qualified medical expenses. Your plan administrator has the final say on what your account covers.

If you don't have health insurance or don't use it for your therapy, the federal No Surprises Act means providers usually must give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost, according to CMS. You may be able to dispute a bill that comes in at least $400 over the estimate.

sections.heading: The sliding scale
paragraphs: Ruzicka Psychology has limited sliding scale slots for self-pay clients. The fee is based on household size and income and ranges from $60 to $225; the income tiers are on the [pricing page](/pricing).
Because the slots are limited, ask about the sliding scale early, in your first email or at the free phone consultation.

sections.heading: If the cost is out of reach
paragraphs: Cost is a real barrier, and it is worth saying out loud. PSI's FAQ notes that many therapists and psychiatrists offer a sliding scale, some may work out a payment plan, and it is fine to ask about adjusting the fee. PSI's local Support Navigators and its HelpLine (1-800-944-4773, not a crisis line) can help you look for lower-cost options. Your insurer's member services line can also list in-network therapists.

Free support is available while you sort it out: PSI's online support groups, and the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), which is free and confidential by call or text, 24/7, and is not a crisis line. See [Support groups or therapy?](/guides/postpartum/support-groups-or-therapy).

Cost should never stop you from getting help in a crisis. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time; it is free and confidential. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. More numbers are on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Will my insurance pay me back for out-of-network therapy?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on your plan. Some plans reimburse part of the cost after a deductible, and some pay nothing out of network. Call your insurer before you start, using the questions above, and keep your monthly superbills.

faqs.question: Is the first session priced differently?
faqs.answer: No. The first session is the same rate as later sessions, $225 for individual therapy. The 15-minute phone consultation before it is free.

faqs.question: Can I use my HSA or FSA?
faqs.answer: Ruzicka Psychology accepts HSA and FSA payments, along with card and check. If you are not sure what your account covers, check with your plan administrator.

pages.metaTitle: Your First Postpartum Therapy Session: What to Expect
pages.metaDescription: What happens before and during a first postpartum therapy session: the consultation call, paperwork, what you talk about, bringing your baby, and how to prep.
pages.summary: A step-by-step look at starting postpartum therapy, from the first email to the end of the first session, and how it works at Ruzicka Psychology.
pages.answer: A first therapy session is mostly a conversation: what brings you in, what you hope will change, and the history that helps make sense of it. You don't need to have it figured out, or the energy to explain it well. At Ruzicka Psychology, a free 15-minute phone consultation and some online paperwork come first, so the first session can focus on you rather than logistics.

sections.heading: Before the first session
paragraphs: Most practices have a few steps before you meet, usually including consent forms. Whoever you see, read them before you sign. They are a good place to find how confidentiality works, the cancellation policy and how to reach the therapist between sessions, and you can ask about anything that is unclear.
Here is how it works at Ruzicka Psychology:
items: You reach out by the [contact form](/contact), by email at Christina@ruzickapsychology.com, or by phone at (585) 667-0970. The form asks only for your name and how to reach you, not health details.
You hear back within 2 business days.
An email covers scheduling, fees, and insurance or payment.
A free 15-minute phone consultation gives you a chance to ask questions and see whether it feels like a fit.

If you go ahead, you get a secure client portal and complete intake paperwork, practice policies and informed-consent forms before the first session. Cancellations need 24 hours' notice, or the full fee applies.

sections.heading: What you will talk about
paragraphs: The first session at Ruzicka Psychology covers what brings you in, your goals, and relevant history. You might mention how pregnancy and birth went, sleep and feeding, support at home, past depression or anxiety, and any medications you take.
ACOG describes talk therapy simply: you and a mental health professional talk about your feelings and discuss how to manage them.

If you have had frightening, unwanted thoughts, you can bring them up. Postpartum Support International (PSI) describes the intrusive thoughts of perinatal OCD as anxious in nature, not a break from reality, and says perinatal OCD is treatable. Get help right away if you are afraid you might act on a thought, or if you or others notice confusion or seeing or hearing things that are not there: call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department, and call or text 988 at any time. See [scary thoughts after having a baby](/guides/postpartum/intrusive-thoughts-after-baby).

sections.heading: You don't need it figured out
paragraphs: You may only know that you feel overwhelmed, flat or unlike yourself. That is enough to start. You don't need a diagnosis either: PSI says you don't need one to reach out for support.

If it helps, jot down a few notes beforehand. PSI notes that some people find it helpful to write down symptoms and feelings before an appointment, and its [discussion tool](https://postpartum.net/discussion-tool/) helps you track symptoms to share with a provider. A few things worth noting:
items: When things started to feel off, and what has changed since
How you are sleeping and eating, beyond what the baby allows
What feels hardest right now, and what you hope will be different
Any medications you take, and the names of your OB/GYN, midwife or doctor
Questions about fees, scheduling or who can attend

sections.heading: Bringing your baby or partner
paragraphs: Ask any therapist about this ahead of time, including what happens if the baby needs feeding or settling. At Ruzicka Psychology, perinatal clients may join virtual sessions with the baby present, and partners and babies may be included in sessions when it is clinically appropriate and supports your goals.

If your partner or your relationship is a big part of what is going on, say so at the consultation. Couples therapy is a separate service, and Christina's couples work draws on Imago Relationship Therapy. See [your relationship after a baby](/guides/postpartum/relationship-after-baby).

sections.heading: In person or online
paragraphs: Individual sessions are a 60-minute block, with 45–50 minutes face to face and 10–15 minutes for documentation and treatment planning.
items: In person: 1577 South Ave, 1st Floor, Rochester, NY 14620. There is a free parking lot attached, RTS Route 13 runs along South Avenue, and the first floor is wheelchair accessible with a portable ramp.

Online: virtual sessions are available across New York through SimplePractice or Zoom, and you need to be physically in New York for each session. With a newborn at home, this can make it easier to show up. More on [online therapy](/specialties/online-therapy).

sections.heading: After the first session
paragraphs: Most clients begin with weekly sessions and may move to every other week later. Some therapy is short-term and focused, some is longer-term, and you review how it is going together.

If medication may help, Christina does not prescribe, but with your signed release of information she can coordinate with your psychiatrist or OB/GYN. If you need crisis care, a high level of care for severe and persistent mental health conditions or eating disorders, or treatment for active addiction, she refers out, and the practice does not provide 24-hour crisis coverage.

If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time. In Monroe County, the UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line is (585) 275-8686, 24/7. The full list is on the [resources page](/resources).

faqs.question: Is the first session free?
faqs.answer: The 15-minute phone consultation is free. The first full session is $225, the same rate as later individual sessions. Details on insurance and the sliding scale are in [paying for postpartum therapy](/guides/postpartum/paying-for-postpartum-therapy-rochester).

faqs.question: What if I cry through the whole session?
faqs.answer: That is okay. You don't need to hold it together or tell your story neatly. The first session is a place to start, not a performance.

faqs.question: What if it doesn't feel like the right fit?
faqs.answer: Say so. The free consultation is partly there to check fit before you commit. If what you need is medication management, crisis care, a high level of care or treatment for active addiction, Ruzicka Psychology is the wrong fit, and Christina refers out for those.

faqs.question: Can I start therapy while I'm still pregnant?
faqs.answer: Yes. Support can begin while trying to conceive, during pregnancy, after a loss, following birth, or at any point in the transition to parenthood. See [depression and anxiety during pregnancy](/guides/postpartum/depression-anxiety-during-pregnancy).

pages.summary: A short list of questions to ask any perinatal therapist before you book, why each one matters, and how Ruzicka Psychology answers them.
pages.answer: Ask about four things: the therapist's license and perinatal training, how they work, the practical details (babies, partners, online sessions, fees and insurance), and what happens if you need more than therapy. Postpartum Support International notes that you have the right and the responsibility to ask about a therapist's qualifications, training, approach and confidentiality. Each question below includes how Ruzicka Psychology answers it.

sections.heading: License and training
paragraphs: Are you licensed in New York, and what is your license number? A license is the baseline, and you can check it on the New York State Office of the Professions [verification search](https://eservices.nysed.gov/professions/verification-search).
How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Dr. Christina Ruzicka, Psy.D., is a Licensed Clinical Psychologist, New York license 024357, practicing as Ruzicka Psychology PLLC.

What perinatal mental health training have you completed? 'Perinatal therapist' is not a license, so ask what is behind the label. PSI's PMH-C credential, for example, requires perinatal training, work experience and a passed exam.
How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Christina has completed Postpartum Support International's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the PMH-C exam.
Who do you work with? This matters if you are not the birthing parent, if your family does not match the textbook picture, or if you are still trying to conceive.

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Adults 18 and older, women and parents across a range of identities and family structures. Support can begin while trying to conceive, during pregnancy, after a loss, following birth, or at any point in the transition to parenthood.

sections.heading: How therapy works
paragraphs: How do you work, and what would sessions with you look like? NIMH names cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy as evidence-based for perinatal depression, and PSI notes other approaches may also be an option. If a specific method matters to you, ask about it by name.
How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Christina's style is relational, psychodynamic, warm and active, with tools from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy when they fit.
How often would we meet, and for how long? This shapes your week and your budget.
How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Most clients begin weekly and may move to every other week later. Length varies from short-term focused work to longer-term therapy, and you review it together.

sections.heading: Babies, partners and where you meet
paragraphs: Can my baby or partner come to sessions? With a newborn, the answer can decide whether therapy is doable at all.

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Partners and babies may be included when it is clinically appropriate and supports your goals, and perinatal clients may join virtual sessions with the baby present. Couples therapy is also offered, and Christina's couples work draws on Imago Relationship Therapy.
Do you offer in-person and online sessions?

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Both. The office is at 1577 South Ave, 1st Floor, Rochester, NY 14620, with a free parking lot attached, RTS Route 13 along South Avenue, and first-floor wheelchair access with a portable ramp. Virtual sessions use SimplePractice or Zoom anywhere in New York, as long as you are physically in New York for each session.

sections.heading: Fees and insurance
paragraphs: What do sessions cost, and do you take my insurance? Ask about the first session, superbills and reduced-fee options too. Only your insurer can tell you what it will reimburse.

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Individual therapy is $225 per 60-minute block (45–50 minutes face to face), and the first session is the same rate. Couples therapy is $275 per 75-minute block. Christina is in network with Aetna through Headway for individual therapy only and takes no other insurance plans. For out-of-network claims, a superbill is sent automatically each month, or weekly on request.
Do you have a sliding scale, and what is your cancellation policy?

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: There are limited sliding scale slots for self-pay clients, based on household size and income, from $60 to $225 (tiers on the [pricing page](/pricing)). Payment is by card, HSA, FSA or check. Cancellations need 24 hours' notice, or the full fee applies. More in [paying for postpartum therapy](/guides/postpartum/paying-for-postpartum-therapy-rochester).

sections.heading: Medication, more care and emergencies
paragraphs: Do you prescribe, and will you work with my doctor? If medication may be part of your care, you want your therapist and prescriber able to talk to each other.
How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Christina does not prescribe. With a signed release of information, she coordinates with psychiatrists and OB/GYNs.
What happens if I need more than weekly therapy, or I am in crisis? Every practice has limits, and it helps to know them before you need them.

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Christina refers out severe and persistent mental health disorders that require a high level of care, eating disorders that require a high level of care, active addiction, and crisis care. The practice does not provide 24-hour crisis coverage.

In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, at any time. The UR Medicine Mental Health Crisis Call Line is (585) 275-8686, 24/7, and more numbers are on the [resources page](/resources).

sections.heading: Getting started
paragraphs: What are the steps to start, and what do you need from me? Knowing the steps takes some of the dread out of reaching out.

How Ruzicka Psychology answers: Get in touch by [contact form](/contact), email or phone; the form asks only for your name and contact details, no health details. You get a reply within 2 business days, then an email about scheduling, fees and insurance or payment, and a free 15-minute phone consultation. If you go ahead, you complete intake paperwork, practice policies and informed-consent forms through a secure client portal before the first session. More on [your first session](/guides/postpartum/first-postpartum-therapy-session).

After any consultation call, notice whether you felt listened to, whether you could imagine telling this person the hard parts, and whether the practical answers were clear. Fit matters alongside credentials.

faqs.question: Is it okay to ask a therapist all of these questions?
faqs.answer: Yes. PSI says you have the right and the responsibility to ask about a therapist's qualifications, training, approach to treatment and confidentiality policies. An email or a free consultation call is a good time to ask.

faqs.question: What does 'approved to take the PMH-C exam' mean?
faqs.answer: In PSI's process, applicants complete the required training and experience, submit documentation and apply. Approved applicants then register for the exam, and those who pass can use PMH-C after their name. Christina has completed PSI's perinatal mental health training and is approved to take the exam. She does not hold the PMH-C credential.

faqs.question: When is Ruzicka Psychology the wrong fit?
faqs.answer: When you need medication management, crisis care or 24-hour coverage, a high level of care for severe and persistent mental health conditions or eating disorders, or treatment for active addiction. Christina refers out for these, and your OB/GYN or doctor can also help you find the right level of care.
